title: Universality and Heterogeneity of Stylized Facts in Cryptocurrency and Equity Markets

p.t: The approval of a spot Bitcoin Exchange-Traded Fund (ETF) by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) in 2024, together with the rapid growth of market capitalization and institutional participation, indicates that cryptocurrencies are no longer peripheral speculative instruments. Major cryptocurrencies now interact with conventional financial institutions, derivatives markets, and systematic trading strategies, while still operating through fragmented exchanges and continuous 24/7 trading. This combination makes them a useful empirical setting for asking whether a market can become statistically mature without becoming dynamically equivalent to traditional financial markets. Classical models for Value-at-Risk (VaR), option pricing, and portfolio allocation often rely on idealized assumptions such as Gaussian returns or independent and identically distributed increments. Empirical studies in econophysics and financial econometrics have repeatedly shown that conventional markets violate these assumptions through heavy-tailed returns, volatility clustering, long memory in activity, and multiscale fluctuations, collectively known as stylized facts [1][2][3][4][5]. These regularities provide model-independent benchmarks for market comparison, because they summarize features directly relevant to tail risk, market efficiency, volatility persistence, and liquidity formation [6,7]. For cryptocurrency markets, the central question has shifted from whether such stylized facts exist to what their apparent convergence with conventional markets actually means. If cryptocurrencies and equity-index futures share heavy tails, near-random-walk return scaling, and persistent absolute returns, their shared statistical properties may suggest that standard trading and pricing models can be applied interchangeably to both markets. However, two return series can display similar distributional and scaling behavior while differing in the temporal organization that produces that behavior. Risk models based only on tail slopes, Hurst exponents, or multifractal widths may therefore miss structural differences associated with nonlinear temporal ordering, local ordinal constraints, or time-directed asymmetry.

Prior research on cryptocurrency stylized facts initially focused on Bitcoin (BTC), documenting power-law-like tails, non-Gaussian return distributions, and long-range memory [8][9][10][11][12]. Later studies identified multifractality in BTC returns [13,14], examined broader cryptocurrency panels, and showed that part of the observed multifractality may arise from broad marginal distributions rather than nonlinear dynamics alone [15]. High-frequency evidence has also suggested that some cryptocurrency markets have matured toward statistical patterns seen in established foreignexchange markets [16]. Nevertheless, a direct comparison with a conventional equity benchmark requires more than documenting the presence of stylized facts. It must separate marginal-distribution effects, linear-correlation effects, and residual temporal structure, especially because intraday seasonality in equity-index futures can otherwise create apparent complexity that is not intrinsic to the return dynamics. This study addresses this issue by treating stylized facts as a starting point rather than as the conclusion of the comparison. We analyze one-minute 2020-2025 data for BTC, Ethereum (ETH), Ripple (XRP), and E-mini S&P 500 futures. To ensure comparability across different trading environments, we mitigate exchange-specific noise in cryptocurrencies via volume-weighted aggregation and apply intraday deseasonalization to all assets to suppress deterministic session artifacts. We then implement a three-layered diagnostic framework to disentangle apparent convergence from structural heterogeneity. First, macroscopic stylized facts, including heavy-tail CCDF and DFA scaling, establish the distributional and correlational properties. Second, multifractal analysis using MF-DFA and surrogate tests identifies the residual scaling heterogeneity that persists beyond linear correlations. Third, structural diagnostics using the complexity-entropy causality plane (CECP) and directed horizontal visibility graph (directed HVG) identify residual heterogeneity in local ordinal patterns and time-directed asymmetry.

The present study therefore seeks to address the following two central questions. 1. To what extent does the apparent convergence of macroscopic stylized facts between mature cryptocurrency markets and traditional equity benchmarks imply a fundamental equivalence in their underlying dynamical processes? 2. Beyond macroscopic statistical similarities, is there a deeper layer of structural heterogeneity in terms of temporal organization and time-irreversibility that persists across these different asset classes? Our results support a layer-dependent interpretation: Coarse-grained similarity coexists with structural heterogeneity. At the macroscopic level, all four assets share heavy-tailed distributions, return Hurst exponents close to the randomwalk benchmark, persistent absolute-return fluctuations, and broadly overlapping MF-DFA curves. The originalsurrogate multifractal-width residual remains positive, but it varies across individual assets rather than producing a simple crypto-equity class separation. However, structural diagnostics reveal a sharper, dual-layered difference in how returns are ordered over time. During ordinary local fluctuations, as captured by the CECP space, cryptocurrencies reside closer to the limit of pure randomness than the equity benchmark, indicating less organized short-run return movements. Conversely, during extreme fluctuations, the directed HVG reveals that the high-visibility sector separates the markets: the S&P 500 becomes largely surrogate-compatible, whereas cryptocurrencies retain a stronger positive high-degree asymmetry. The contribution of this paper is therefore methodological and empirical. Methodologically, we combine highfrequency data with equity-index intraday deseasonalization, surrogate decomposition, CECP, and directed-HVG diagnostics into a unified framework for distinguishing macroscopic convergence from structural equivalence. Empirically, we show that post-2020 cryptocurrency markets cannot be characterized simply as immature versions of traditional markets or as fully converged counterparts. Instead, they align with traditional benchmarks in broad stylized facts while being more random-looking during ordinary fluctuations and more asymmetric around large, high-visibility events.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the data window, the intradaydeseasonalization protocol, and the analytical methodology. Section 3 establishes the standard stylized facts and their limits as a structural classifier. Section 4 then applies surrogate-controlled CECP and directed-HVG diagnostics to test residual crypto-equity heterogeneity. Section 5 discusses the implication that macroscopic similarity does not entail structural equivalence and concludes the paper.

We analyze high-frequency trading data for three major cryptocurrencies-Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH), and Ripple (XRP)-sourced from major global USD exchanges (Bitstamp, Coinbase, and Kraken), with per-exchange data coverage summarized in Table S1 of the Supplementary Material. The E-mini S&P 500 futures contract (CME) serves as the conventional equity benchmark (hereafter referred to simply as the S&P 500). The analysis period for all assets spans from January 1, 2020, to December 31, 2025, a window where cryptocurrency stylized facts have been shown to occupy a stable, mature regime. Rolling-window DFA, volatility-autocorrelation, and GARCH(1,1) parameter-distance diagnostics computed over 2015-2025 show that BTC, ETH, and XRP converge onto the S&P 500's dispersion band around 2019-2020, with XRP the slowest asset to transition (Figs. S1-S2; Sec. S5 of the Supplementary Material for the full diagnostic protocol). Let 𝑃 𝑡 represent the price of a cryptocurrency at time 𝑡. The log-return over a 1-min interval is defined as 𝑟 𝑡 = ln(𝑃 𝑡 ∕𝑃 𝑡-1 ). To mitigate venue-specific microstructure noise, the cryptocurrency returns r𝑡 are computed via volume-weighted aggregation across the selected exchanges: where 𝑟 𝑡,𝑖 and 𝑉 𝑡,𝑖 denote the return and trading volume of the 𝑖-th venue. The absolute return |𝑟 𝑡 | is used as the proxy for volatility. Continuous time series are constructed by removing non-trading intervals and missing values. For the S&P 500, artificial price discontinuities arising from contract rollovers are eliminated through a standard backward-adjustment procedure [17]. Specifically, at each rollover point, we calculate the price ratio 𝑅 = 𝑃 next ∕𝑃 current and adjust all prior prices by this factor to ensure that log-returns reflect only intrinsic market movements rather than contract basis shifts. To ensure a robust comparison between 24/7 cryptocurrency trading and the session-based equity market, we applied a minute-of-day volatility deseasonalization to all assets [3]:

where 𝑚(𝑡) is the minute-of-day index and σ𝑚 is the Gaussian-smoothed standard deviation of absolute returns at that intraday minute. This procedure suppresses deterministic trading-cycle artifacts while preserving intrinsic dynamical structures. Subsequent analyses operate on these deseasonalized series r𝑡 .

To establish the shared distributional properties, we characterize the upper tail of absolute returns using the complementary cumulative distribution function (CCDF): where 𝛼 denotes the Pareto tail exponent. The exponent 𝛼 is estimated via maximum likelihood following the Clauset-Shalizi-Newman procedure [18]. The lower threshold 𝑥 min is determined by minimizing the Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance between the empirical and fitted distributions. These estimates provide a reference for macroscopic tail risk similarity rather than a definitive ranking of market convergence.

p.s: Detrended Fluctuation and Multifractal Scaling Analysis
p.t: To quantify temporal correlations and scale-dependent heterogeneity while reducing the influence of local trends, we used detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA) and its multifractal extension (MF-DFA) [19][20][21][22][23]. DFA divides the integrated time series into windows of size 𝑠, removes polynomial trends within each window, and measures the fluctuation function 𝐹 (𝑠). For a self-similar process, where the Hurst exponent 𝐻 ≈ 0.5 corresponds to an uncorrelated process, while 𝐻 > 0.5 and 𝐻 < 0.5 indicate persistent and anti-persistent correlations, respectively. We applied DFA to returns 𝑟 𝑡 , absolute returns |𝑟 𝑡 |, and trading volume 𝑉 𝑡 to examine market efficiency, volatility clustering, and persistence in trading activity, respectively. Throughout the DFA and MF-DFA analyses, we used second-order polynomial detrending over the scaling range 𝑠 = 10 1 -10 4 minutes. 1 To examine whether small and 1 Using linear detrending instead did not materially affect the main conclusions. large fluctuations obey different scaling laws, we applied MF-DFA by varying the moment order 𝑞 over [-4, 4]. The generalized Hurst exponent ℎ(𝑞) was estimated from 𝐹 𝑞 (𝑠) ∼ 𝑠 ℎ (𝑞) . From the generalized Hurst exponent, the multifractal spectrum 𝑓 (𝛼) is obtained via a Legendre transform of the mass exponent 𝜏(𝑞) = 𝑞ℎ(𝑞) -1: where 𝛼 is the singularity strength. The spectrum width Δ𝛼 = 𝛼 max -𝛼 min was used as a scalar measure of multifractality, with larger values indicating stronger heterogeneity in local scaling behaviors.

To characterize the ordinal information structure and nonlinear dynamics, we employed the complexity-entropy causality plane (CECP) [24] based on Bandt-Pompe patterns [25]. This symbolic approach maps continuous returns onto a sequence of discrete permutations, effectively capturing temporal organization while remaining robust against heavy-tailed marginal distributions. The ordinal patterns, defined by embedding dimension 𝐷 and delay 𝜏, yield a distribution 𝑃 of permutations. The normalized permutation entropy 𝐻[𝑃 ], quantifying the degree of disorder, is: where 𝐷! is the number of possible states and 𝑝(𝜋) is the probability of each possible permutation (see Eq. S3). The statistical complexity 𝐶[𝑃 ] measures non-trivial structural organization: where 𝑃 𝑒 is the uniform distribution and 𝑄 𝐽 is the normalized Jensen-Shannon divergence. 𝐶[𝑃 ] vanishes in the limits of pure randomness (𝐻 → 1) and pure order (𝐻 → 0), identifying structured dynamics between these poles. We used 𝐷 = 5 and 𝜏 = 1, ensuring robust estimates with 3 × 10 6 observations (see Sec. S2 of the Supplementary Material for technical details).

To quantify temporal asymmetry in market returns, we used the directed horizontal visibility graph (directed HVG) [26,27]. This approach characterizes time-series irreversibility by comparing in-degree and out-degree distributions using information-theoretic divergences. Previous studies demonstrated that financial irreversibility fluctuates over time, clusters during market stress, and provides information complementary to standard volatility [28]. In this study, we analyzed directed-HVG irreversibility by decomposing the in/out-degree asymmetry into three complementary components: (i) the magnitude of asymmetry, (ii) its directional orientation, and (iii) the degree-local concentration. Figure 1 illustrates the HVG construction. A directed edge was assigned from node 𝑖 to 𝑗 (𝑖 < 𝑗) if no intermediate observation blocked their horizontal line-of-sight: For a graph with 𝑁 nodes, the empirical in-and out-degree distributions are where 𝑘 in 𝑖 and 𝑘 out 𝑖 are the in-and out-degrees of node 𝑖, respectively, and 𝟏(⋅) is the indicator function. For a time-reversible process, the forward and backward visibility structures are expected to be statistically equivalent. Any discrepancy therefore indicates statistical time irreversibility, meaning that the forward and backward visibility structures are not equivalent. The Kullback-Leibler divergence between two discrete distributions 𝑃 and 𝑄 is defined as To capture the magnitude of this discrepancy, we employed the Jensen-Shannon divergence (𝐷 JS ): where 𝑀(𝑘) = 1 2 [𝑃 in (𝑘) + 𝑃 out (𝑘)] is the mean degree distribution. Conceptually, 𝐷 JS determines whether the return series exhibits disparate visibility statistics when viewed forward versus backward in time. Thus, 𝐷 JS = 0 indicates identical in-and out-degree distributions, whereas larger values indicate a stronger in-out distributional mismatch.

However, because 𝐷 JS is symmetric, it does not identify which temporal side of the event drives the mismatch. To retain this directional information, we also used the normalized signed KL imbalance (𝐴 KL ), Because empirical degree distributions can contain zero-probability bins, direct KL ratios may become unstable or undefined for degrees observed in only one direction. Before computing the KL-based quantities, the in-and outdegree histograms were therefore regularized by adding a pseudocount of 0.5 to each retained degree bin and then renormalizing the two histograms to probability distributions. The normalization by the sum of both KL directions isolates the orientation of the mismatch from its magnitude. A positive 𝐴 KL indicates that the in-degree distribution is less well represented by the out-degree distribution, whereas a negative value indicates the opposite. Because edge direction follows time, this sign identifies whether the mismatch is weighted toward backward-or forward-visibility configurations and reverses under time reversal. It does not, by itself, identify a unique buildup-recovery path. Finally, we examined the degree-local asymmetry profile, 𝐴(𝑘) decomposes the signed asymmetry by degree. At a given degree, 𝐴(𝑘) > 0 means that nodes with 𝑘 backward links occur more frequently than nodes with 𝑘 forward links; the opposite holds when 𝐴(𝑘) < 0. This allows us to distinguish between imbalances arising from typical low-degree fluctuations and those concentrated in high-visibility return configurations.

To provide a common operational definition across assets and return transforms, 𝐷 JS and 𝐴 KL are recomputed over the high-degree sector (𝑘 ≥ 10). Degree-wise Fisher exact tests show that this threshold lies within the range where sustained crypto-equity separation emerges for raw, absolute, and positive returns, whereas the negative-returnmagnitude results are more asset-specific (Sec. S8 and Fig. S7). Details of the network construction and divergence estimation are provided in Sec. S3 of the Supplementary Material. We first construct the DHVG from the raw signed-return series {𝑟 𝑡 }. To identify what drives the directional asymmetry, we repeat the analysis for the absolute-return series {|𝑟 𝑡 |}, the positive-return subsequence {𝑟 𝑡 ∶ 𝑟 𝑡 > 0}, and the negative-return-magnitude subsequence {-𝑟 𝑡 ∶ 𝑟 𝑡 < 0}. The absolute-return series keeps every observation on the original clock-time grid but removes its sign. The sign-conditioned subsequences keep only positive returns or the magnitudes of negative returns in their original occurrence order and do not preserve the elapsed time between them.

To isolate the statistical origins of the observed market dynamics, we applied a surrogate-based decomposition to the MF-DFA, CECP, and HVG-based diagnostics. By recomputing these measures for surrogate ensembles, we can disentangle the respective contributions of marginal distributions, linear correlations, and nonlinear temporal structures. We used two types of surrogate data. Shuffled surrogates preserve the marginal distribution of the original series while removing temporal dependence. Iterative amplitude-adjusted Fourier transform (IAAFT) surrogates preserve both the marginal distribution and the linear autocorrelation structure while disrupting nonlinear phase relationships [29]. Thus, differences between the original series and shuffled surrogates indicate the contribution of temporal ordering beyond the marginal distribution, whereas differences from IAAFT surrogates indicate nonlinear temporal structure beyond the linear spectrum. For each asset and each surrogate type, we generated 100 realizations and recomputed the relevant diagnostic measures. The original estimates were then compared with the corresponding surrogate ensembles, using ensembleaveraged values and the dispersion across realizations. For HVG asymmetry, this dispersion was computed at the level of the final diagnostic: for each surrogate realization 𝑠, we first evaluated 𝐴 (𝑠) KL from its own pair of KL divergences and then reported the mean and standard deviation of {𝐴 (𝑠) KL }. This procedure allowed us to distinguish distributional, linear-correlation, and nonlinear temporal contributions to the observed market dynamics. Details of the surrogategeneration algorithms are provided in Sec. S4 of the Supplementary Material.

We begin by characterizing the stylized facts across the cryptocurrencies and the S&P 500 benchmark to evaluate the extent of their statistical overlap and identify where they leave room for structural diagnostics. Accordingly, we conduct a heavy-tail analysis and estimate global Hurst exponents using second-order detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA-2). In the heavy-tail analysis, we use the maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) based power-law fit following the Clauset-Shalizi-Newman procedure [18] to check whether all four assets occupy a common fat-tailed regime. Figure 2 summarizes these tail characteristics, plotting the cumulative probability 𝑃 (|r| > 𝑥) against the return threshold 𝑥 on a double-logarithmic scale. As shown in panel (a), the one-minute empirical complementary cumulative distribution functions (CCDFs) of all four assets decay much slower than a Gaussian (black solid line), confirming the presence of heavy-tailed returns. The tail exponents estimated from the maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) fits fall in the range 𝛼 ≈ 2.5-2.9. In the econophysics literature, this is close to the inverse cubic law of return distributions (𝛼 ≈ 3.0), which describes the universal scale-invariant tail behavior observed across diverse financial markets [1,2]. Our results indicate that cryptocurrencies (BTC, ETH, and XRP) have converged to the same fat-tailed regime as traditional equity index futures, violating Gaussian modeling assumptions. Panels (b) and (c) display the scale dependence of the tail behavior for Bitcoin and the S&P 500, respectively. As the aggregation interval increases from 1 to 60 minutes (indicated by the purple-to-yellow transition), both assets exhibit a rightward shift in their CCDFs. For Bitcoin (panel b), the tail exponent exhibits a moderate increase from 𝛼 ≈ 2.8 to 𝛼 ≈ 3.3, indicating a gradual onset of aggregational Gaussianity. In contrast, the S&P 500 exponent (panel c) remains stable around 𝛼 ≈ 2.4-2.6, showing no pronounced change within this short aggregation range. Crucially, due to strong temporal dependence, this convergence toward the Gaussian attractor is extremely slow for both assets, keeping them well within the heavy-tailed regime (𝛼 < 4) even at the hourly scale. This shows that rather than displaying distinct risk profiles, both markets share a common distributional structure where extreme tail events occur with comparable scaling probabilities. Table S2 confirms that this heavy-tailed regime persists under a stricter post-2022 window. The S&P 500 slope shifts closer to the inverse-cubic benchmark in this window, underscoring the sensitivity of 𝛼 to the sample choice.

We next use detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA) to test whether global monofractal scaling separates the asset classes. The focus is on whether price directionality, volatility clustering, and trading activity exhibit common scaling patterns. Table 1 summarizes the log-log slopes of the fluctuation functions as global Hurst exponents (𝐻) and compares their temporal origins using Shuffle and IAAFT surrogate tests.

Global Hurst exponents (𝐻) estimated by DFA-2 with second-order polynomial detrending. The table summarizes the Hurst exponents for returns (𝑟 𝑡 ), absolute returns (|𝑟 𝑡 |), and trading volume (𝑉 𝑡 ) for Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH), Ripple (XRP), and the S&P 500 benchmark. Errors (±) denote the standard error (SE) of the log-log linear regression slope; the Shuffled and IAAFT errors are the SEs from linear regressions fitted to the 100-realization ensemble-mean fluctuation functions. Returns remain close to the random-walk 𝐻 ≈ 0.5, consistent with the absence of linear autocorrelation, whereas absolute returns and trading volume exhibit strong long-memory behavior with 𝐻 ≫ 0.5.

For the return series, the original exponents (𝐻 orig ) and both surrogate results (𝐻 shuf , 𝐻 IAAFT ) all cluster tightly around the theoretical random-walk benchmark (𝐻 = 0.5), hovering in the narrow range of 0.49-0.51. This confirms the macroscopic absence of linear autocorrelations in returns across both asset classes, showing that they behave as directionally unpredictable, weak-form efficient random walks.

By contrast, absolute returns and trading volume both exhibit strong long-range persistence across all assets. Specifically, the original Hurst exponents are consistently high for both absolute returns (𝐻 orig ≈ 0.90-0.92) and trading volume (𝐻 orig ≈ 0.81-0.93), demonstrating persistent volatility clustering and trading activity. For both metrics, this long-range correlation is entirely destroyed by shuffling (𝐻 shuf ≈ 0.51) but preserved by the IAAFT surrogates (𝐻 IAAFT ≈ 𝐻 orig ). This confirms that both volatility memory and volume persistence are linear autocorrelation features governed by the power spectrum of the respective series, establishing a baseline of macroscopic convergence where cryptocurrencies share a common scaling regime with traditional equity benchmarks.

Since these single-scale Hurst exponents cannot resolve the finer, scale-dependent or nonlinear temporal structures beneath the surface, their statistical similarity confirms macroscopic convergence but does not guarantee structural equivalence. We therefore apply multifractal detrended fluctuation analysis (MF-DFA) with Shuffle and IAAFT surrogate tests to examine this scale-dependent heterogeneity. By comparing the empirical scaling behaviors of the original series against their shuffled and IAAFT surrogate ensembles, this approach disentangles the relative contributions of marginal distributions, linear correlations, and nonlinear temporal dynamics. These comparison results are presented in Figure 3 and Table 2. 3 compares the MF-DFA results of the original return series against their IAAFT and Shuffle surrogates across two representations: the generalized Hurst exponent ℎ(𝑞) and the multifractal spectrum 𝑓 (𝛼). For the original data, the monotonic decrease in ℎ(𝑞) and the broad, concave 𝑓 (𝛼) spectrum confirm multifractal scaling across all assets. In contrast, both surrogate ensembles produce substantially flatter ℎ(𝑞) curves and significantly narrower spectra. The close overlap between the Shuffle and IAAFT curves indicates that the surrogates' remaining scaling behavior is primarily driven by the marginal distribution of returns, while the displacement between the original and IAAFT curves reflects residual temporal organization. These scaling properties are quantitatively summarized in Table 2. For all assets, negative moments yield scaling exponents above the random-walk benchmark (ℎ(-3) > 0.5), indicating persistence in small-scale fluctuations, whereas positive moments fall below this threshold (ℎ(3) < 0.5), indicating anti-persistent dynamics for largescale fluctuations. Bitcoin exhibits the strongest 𝑞-dependence and the widest spectrum (Δ𝛼 = 0.7000), followed by Ethereum (0.5197), while XRP (0.3505) and the S&P 500 (0.3292) show much narrower spectra. By comparison, the Shuffle and IAAFT surrogates hover near the mono-scaling benchmark (ℎ(𝑞) ≈ 0.5) and yield remarkably consistent spectrum widths (Δ𝛼 ≈ 0.23-0.25) across all assets. Since both surrogate methods yield similar spectrum widths despite preserving different temporal properties, this baseline width is a statistical artifact caused solely by the heavytailed distribution of returns. Therefore, the significantly wider spectra observed in the original data confirm that the assets' multifractality is driven by genuine temporal dynamics rather than simple distributional properties or linear correlations.

To isolate these contributions, we decompose the empirical generalized Hurst exponent as ℎ orig (𝑞) = ℎ shuf (𝑞) + Δ lin (𝑞) + Δ nl (𝑞), where ℎ shuf (𝑞) represents the contribution of the marginal distribution, Δ lin (𝑞) = ℎ IAAFT (𝑞) -ℎ shuf (𝑞) quantifies the effect of linear autocorrelation, and Δ nl (𝑞) = ℎ orig (𝑞) -ℎ IAAFT (𝑞) measures the multifractality arising from nonlinear temporal correlations (such as volatility clustering). This decomposition reveals that nonlinear multifractality is present in all assets but differs substantially in magnitude. The nonlinear component, measured by the difference between the empirical and IAAFT spectrum widths, reaches 0.4460 for BTC and 0.2927 for ETH, compared with only 0.1195 for XRP and 0.0764 for the S&P 500. Likewise, the empirical multifractal width varies more strongly across individual assets than across the simple cryptocurrency-equity distinction, with XRP exhibiting scaling characteristics closer to the S&P 500 than to BTC. These results indicate that MF-DFA captures meaningful asset-specific nonlinear scaling structures but does not by itself provide a clear asset-class separation. Figure S3 confirms that BTC retains the broadest spectrum under a stricter post-2022 window, though the relative ordering of ETH, XRP, and S&P 500 is not preserved as ETH's spectrum narrows the most. The shuffle and IAAFT surrogates remain in close agreement in this window as well, consistent with MF-DFA's use as a sensitivity diagnostic rather than a crypto-equity discriminator. This observation motivates the subsequent ordinal-pattern and visibility-network analyses, which examine temporal organization beyond conventional multifractal scaling.

While the four assets share common stylized facts-including heavy-tailed distributions, volatility clustering, and similar multifractal scaling properties-the discrepancies between original and IAAFT results in the MF-DFA indicate that residual temporal structures persist beyond what linear correlations can explain. We therefore employ the complexity-entropy causality plane (CECP) and the directed horizontal visibility graph (DHVG) to probe structural differences that remain hidden from these global indicators. By comparing the original series against both Shuffle surrogates (which preserve only the marginal distribution) and IAAFT surrogates (which preserve the linear power spectrum), we can isolate non-temporal distribution effects from genuine nonlinear and time-directed temporal organization.

We examine short-horizon ordinal structure in the (1 -𝐻, 𝐶) plane, where proximity to the origin indicates higher entropy and weaker symbolic organization. Results are reported for 𝐷 = 5 and 𝜏 = 1. Figure 4(a) shows the original asset returns in the (1 -𝐻, 𝐶) plane. The permutation entropy 𝐻 measures the diversity and evenness of ordinal patterns, reaching its maximum when all possible patterns occur equally often. The statistical complexity 𝐶 is low when the pattern distribution is either uniform or dominated by a single pattern, and becomes larger when multiple patterns occur with unequal frequencies. BTC, ETH, and XRP cluster near the highentropy, low-complexity boundary (𝐻 → 1, 𝐶 → 0), indicating greater local ordinal randomness. Although XRP is slightly displaced from BTC and ETH, the three cryptocurrencies remain clearly separated from the S&P 500, which has a larger entropy deficit (1 -𝐻 ≈ 21.0 × 10 -4 ) and statistical complexity (𝐶 ≈ 37.2 × 10 -4 ). In Figure S6, the asset ordering underlying this separation remains stable across a broader 𝐷 ∈ {3, … , 7}, 𝜏 ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5, 10} embedding grid. The surrogate analysis in Figure 4(b) clarifies the statistical origins of this separation by comparing 1 -𝐻 and 𝐶 across original, shuffled, and IAAFT surrogate ensembles. Under shuffling, the cryptocurrency coordinates approach the random limit, whereas the S&P 500 retains a non-zero baseline (1-𝐻 ≈ 8.1×10 -4 , 𝐶 ≈ 14. 4×10 -4 ). This residual baseline is consistent with the higher frequency of zero-return intervals in the S&P 500 series, which is preserved by shuffling and produces repeated ordinal ties.

The IAAFT comparison further isolates the role of linear autocorrelations. For BTC and ETH, the IAAFT surrogates reproduce most of the original complexity and entropy deficit, indicating a greater contribution from linear correlations than for XRP. For XRP, the IAAFT coordinates lie closer to the shuffled baseline than those of BTC and ETH, indicating a smaller contribution from linear correlations. Its correspondingly larger original-IAAFT gap is consistent with a greater contribution from nonlinear temporal correlations. For the S&P 500, the Shuffle and IAAFT baselines are nearly identical, while a substantial original-IAAFT gap remains (𝐶 orig -𝐶 IAAFT ≈ 22.2 × 10 -4 ), indicating nonlinear ordinal structure not captured by the linear spectrum or marginal distribution. In Figure S4, the cross-asset CECP hierarchy and its surrogate-based decomposition are both preserved under a stricter post-2022 window.

Having established differences in local ordinal structure, we use the Directed Horizontal Visibility Graph (DHVG) to examine how time irreversibility varies with node degree. Unlike the CECP, which characterizes local symbolic ordering, the DHVG maps relative visibility and identifies the high-degree observations that dominate temporal asymmetry. Restricting the analysis to the high-degree sector sharpens the crypto-equity contrast: cryptocurrency 𝐷 JS remains above the surrogate baselines and 𝐴 KL shifts further positive, whereas the S&P 500 𝐷 JS falls within the surrogate range and 𝐴 KL shifts from near zero to negative. In Figure 5(a), the observed 𝐷 JS exceeds both surrogate baselines for every asset over all degrees, showing aggregate irreversibility not reproduced by the controls. The nearly overlapping shuffled and IAAFT baselines indicate little additional contribution from linear temporal correlations. At this aggregate level, however, 𝐷 JS does not clearly separate cryptocurrencies from the S&P 500. The degree-wise curves first identify where the crypto-equity separation occurs. Figure 5(c) shows that 𝐴(𝑘) remains near zero at low degrees but rises sharply for cryptocurrencies at 𝑘 ≥ 10, while the S&P 500 curve remains comparatively flat. Restricting 𝐷 JS to this high-degree sector sharpens the contrast visible in Figure 5(a): the cryptocurrency values remain above both surrogate baselines, whereas the S&P 500 value falls within the surrogate range. The corresponding 𝐴 KL comparison shows that restricting the analysis to high-degree nodes also sharpens the directional separation. Over all degrees, 𝐴 KL is positive for the cryptocurrencies but remains near zero for the S&P 500. At 𝑘 ≥ 10, all three cryptocurrency values shift further in the positive direction; Bitcoin and XRP exceed the surrogate error bars, while Ethereum remains positive but within them. The S&P 500, by contrast, shifts into negative territory in Figure 5(b) and falls below the surrogate ranges. In DHVG terms, the positive high-degree 𝐴 KL indicates greater visibility toward the past than toward the future. In Figure S5, the crypto-equity 𝐷 JS contrast and the high-degree 𝐴 KL orientation remain qualitatively unchanged under a stricter post-2022 window, although XRP's separation from the surrogate ranges narrows.

The raw-return analysis combines positive and negative moves, so it cannot determine whether this asymmetric event path is driven by volatility magnitude or by a particular return sign. Figure 6 separates these contributions using absolute returns, positive-return subsequences, and negative-return-magnitude subsequences. Sign-conditioned subsequences retain the order of same-sign returns after removing opposite-sign observations, but not the elapsed time between retained observations. For absolute and positive returns, all three cryptocurrencies remain above the surrogate ranges at both degree ranges, while the S&P 500 remains within them. For negative-return magnitudes, all three cryptocurrencies exceed the all-degree surrogate ranges, but only Ethereum and XRP remain above them at high degrees. In Figure 6(a), absolute-return 𝐴 KL exceeds both surrogate ranges for all three cryptocurrencies and increases when the analysis is restricted to 𝑘 ≥ 10, whereas the S&P 500 remains within those ranges. The stronger positive shift after return signs are removed indicates that return magnitude contributes to the high-degree asymmetry. Its separation from the IAAFT baselines further shows that the marginal distribution and linear spectrum preserved by these surrogates do not reproduce the observed ordering. Figure 6(b) shows the same pattern for the positive-return subsequences: all three cryptocurrencies exceed the surrogate error bars over both the full and high-degree distributions, with 𝐴 KL shifting further positive at 𝑘 ≥ 10. Within the retained positive-return ordering, this high-degree shift corresponds to large gains being followed by a denser ordering of subsequent gains. Because opposite-sign observations and elapsed time are removed, this result does not imply an uninterrupted rally in clock time.

For negative-return magnitudes, Figure 6(c) shows that all three cryptocurrencies exceed the surrogate ranges over the full degree distribution. At 𝑘 ≥ 10, Ethereum and XRP remain above those ranges, whereas Bitcoin falls within them; the S&P 500 remains within the surrogate ranges at both degree levels. Within the retained negative-return ordering, the high-degree asymmetry therefore persists for Ethereum and XRP but not for Bitcoin, making its lossside contribution asset-dependent. The corresponding degree-resolved 𝐷 JS , 𝐴 KL , and 𝐴(𝑘) results for all three return transformations are provided in Fig. S7.

This study examined whether the macroscopic similarities between cryptocurrencies and the S&P 500 extend to their temporal organization. Distributional, DFA, and MF-DFA analyses showed that all four assets share heavy-tailed returns, volatility clustering, and multifractal scaling. The strength of multifractality, however, varied more across individual assets than between cryptocurrencies and the equity benchmark. Since these measures did not clearly separate the two asset classes, we next examined short-horizon temporal structure using surrogate-controlled CECP and DHVG analyses. The CECP revealed weaker local ordinal organization in cryptocurrencies than in the S&P 500, whereas the DHVG localized the crypto-equity separation to high-visibility events. These findings show that similarity in conventional statistics does not imply equivalent short-horizon temporal organization. The CECP surrogate comparisons show that the sources of local ordinal organization differ across assets. This heterogeneity may reflect distinct trading environments. Standardized execution and liquidity provision can generate recurrent ordering in equity-index returns, whereas fragmented and continuously operating cryptocurrency markets may weaken such regularities. The DHVG results reveal that the weaker local ordinal organization of cryptocurrencies coexists with stronger directional asymmetry around high-visibility events. This asymmetry is consistent with quiet pre-event paths followed by denser activity. Its persistence after sign removal and beyond the IAAFT baseline links it to volatility magnitude and nonlinear temporal organization. Sign conditioning reveals a shared upside but an asset-dependent downside component.

Together, these results reveal layered market maturation. The cryptocurrencies studied here are less locally organized during ordinary fluctuations yet more directionally asymmetric around high-visibility events. Models that reproduce tails, volatility clustering, and scaling can still miss the event-ordering structure that differentiates cryptocurrencies from the equity benchmark. Model adequacy should therefore be assessed against the CECP coordinates and DHVG signatures 𝐷 JS , 𝐴 KL , and 𝐴(𝑘), rather than conventional stylized facts alone.

The CECP separation reported in the main text is stable across a broad short-memory embedding grid. The main CECP analysis uses embedding dimension 𝑚 = 5 and delay 𝜏 = 1. To verify that the crypto-equity separation is not an artifact of this production choice, we recomputed the CECP coordinates over an embedding grid 𝑚 ∈ {3, 4, 5, 6, 7}, 𝜏 ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5, 10}. The grid search was performed for both the post-2020 production window and the post-2022 robustness window, using the same deseasonalized returns and surrogate settings as in the main CECP analysis. Figure S6 summarizes the separation by two ratios. The first is the statistical-complexity ratio, 𝐶 S&P ∕ max(𝐶 crypto ). The second is the entropy-deficit ratio, (1 -𝐻) S&P ∕ max(1 -𝐻) crypto . Values above one mean that the S&P 500 has higher complexity, or a larger departure from maximum permutation entropy, than every cryptocurrency at the same (𝑚, 𝜏). The result is uniform across the grid. In the post-2020 window, the S&P 500 has the highest 𝐶 and the largest entropy deficit across all 25 tested parameter combinations; the same pattern holds in the post-2022 window. This grid check supports the interpretation that the CECP result reflects a stable short-lag ordinal-structure difference rather than a parameter-tuning artifact. The strength of the separation varies across embedding choices, but the direction of the separation does not change over the tested range.
